title: The light we cannot see.
teaser: Two paper stars send Little searching beyond the rainbow.
question: Why does one star glow and the other stay quiet?
idea: A black light gives out mostly UV-A, a kind of ultraviolet light our eyes cannot see. Some materials, including phosphors and fluorescent dyes, absorb that light and quickly emit visible light. This re-glow is fluorescence.

curiosity.intro: Two stars. One small mystery. Choose a question and search the picture for a clue.
curiosity.carryForward: Follow the discovery through six scenes. Then arrange a little light model and give the glow your own words.

questions.question: Why does only one star glow?
questions.notice: Find the two paper stars. What looks the same? What looks different? Keep a guess before opening the explanation.
questions.say: The glowing star has a fluorescent coating. It takes in light from the black light and gives out green light we can see. The other star has no coating that makes a noticeable glow in this model. Shape alone does not decide which object glows.
questions.try: Point to the part you would change to test your guess in a drawing: the lamp, the star's shape, or its material.

questions.question: Can light reach a place our eyes cannot see?
questions.notice: Follow the rainbow to its violet end. The small dark patch sits just beyond it. What might a change in the paper tell us?
questions.say: In 1801, Johann Ritter found that light-sensitive material changed beyond the violet end of a spread-out rainbow. Something unseen was reaching it. We call that light ultraviolet, or UV. UV-A is the part near visible violet that ordinary black lights use. UV-A itself is invisible to our eyes.
questions.try: Trace the rainbow in the picture. Pause at violet, then point just beyond it. Imagine finding a clue without seeing what made it.

questions.question: Is a black light really sending out darkness?
questions.notice: Look at the lamp's dim violet face and the space beneath it. A picture cannot show invisible light directly. What could reveal its presence?
questions.say: A black light sends out mostly UV-A light. A little visible violet can leak out too; that is the purple we see at the lamp. The invisible UV-A is not darkness. A suitable fluorescent material can help us notice what the lamp is doing.
questions.try: Imagine putting the two drawn stars beneath this lamp. Tell which clue you would watch for. The screen model is enough.

questions.question: How can a material make a new color of light?
questions.notice: The lens enlarges the star's coating. Follow the idea from lamp to coating to green glow. Where is the visible light coming from?
questions.say: A phosphor is a material that can take in energy and give out light. Here a fluorescent phosphor takes in UV-A and quickly gives out visible green light. Some fluorescent dyes do this too. The quick re-glow is called fluorescence. Different materials can glow in different colors, or show no glow under this lamp.
questions.try: Tell a three-part path using these words: UV-A in, material, visible light out. Draw arrows if they help.

reading.title: The light we cannot see
reading.coverText: Two stars rest under a dark-looking lamp. Only one shines. Little follows the clue.
reading.parentNote: About 15 minutes: share the six scenes and two questions. Read aloud for Leo; pointing and spoken answers count. Historical scenes are imagined museum displays. The foldable contains this same story.

beats.title: Two paper stars
beats.passage: A green star shines in a quiet museum case. Beside it, a cream star stays dull. Both sit under the same dark-looking lamp. “Is one full of tiny lights?” Little asks. Big leans closer. The two stars have left them a puzzle.
beats.prompt: What would you compare first? Keep your guess.

beats.title: Beyond violet
beats.passage: Their search begins long ago. In 1801, Johann Ritter spread sunlight into a rainbow. Light-sensitive material darkened just beyond violet, where he could see no light. An unseen kind of light was there! Today we call it ultraviolet, or UV. “A clue past the rainbow,” Little says.
beats.prompt: How did Ritter find a clue to light he could not see?

beats.title: A name for the glow
beats.passage: Another display tells of George Stokes. In 1852, he studied materials that took in light and gave out a different color. He called the glow fluorescence. A crystal gleams blue in the case. “Could our star be doing that?” Little wonders. The old discoveries offer a new clue.
beats.prompt: What name did Stokes give this kind of glow?

beats.title: A dark-looking light
beats.passage: Back at the stars, Little studies the black light. It gives out mostly UV-A, the ultraviolet near visible violet. Our eyes cannot see UV-A. A little visible violet makes the lamp look purple. “It isn't sending out darkness,” Little says. “It's sending light we cannot see!”
beats.prompt: Is the purple we see the invisible UV-A?

beats.title: Light in, light out
beats.passage: The green star has a special coating: a fluorescent phosphor. It absorbs UV-A and quickly emits green light. Absorb means take in; emit means give out. That re-glow is fluorescence. The plain star lacks this coating. “Same shape, different material!” Little says. The glow comes from the star itself.
beats.prompt: Follow the light into the coating and back out. What changes?

beats.title: Keep the clue
beats.passage: The museum lamp switches off. The green fluorescence stops almost at once. Little sketches a lamp, a star, and light coming out. “No tiny lights inside,” Little says. “A material makes the re-glow.” Big leaves room on the page. What other material might hold a clue?

outline.arc: Two stars pose a mystery; Ritter discovers unseen UV; Stokes names fluorescence; Little follows UV-A from lamp into coating and visible light out; lamp off resolves the first guess.

beatIntents.intent: Wonder at matching shapes with different glow.
Ritter finds unseen light through a material change.
Stokes gives fluorescence a name, without claiming he invented black lights.
Distinguish invisible UV-A from visible violet leakage.
Coating absorbs UV-A and emits visible green light.
Prompt stopping of fluorescence resolves the tiny-lights guess.

math.title: A little strip of light
math.intro: Our pretend spectrum strip has seven named places. Start at UV-A and move toward red. The numbers show positions, not measurements.
math.printNote: UV-A is unseen. The other six names are visible colors. Real colors blend; these boxes are not equal measured bands.

tasks.label: COUNT THE VISIBLE PLACES
tasks.prompt: There are 7 places. One is unseen UV-A. How many places name visible colors?
tasks.hint: Count the names from violet through red.

tasks.label: HOP ALONG
tasks.prompt: Start at place 1, UV-A. How many one-place hops reach place 7, red?
tasks.hint: Count the gaps you cross, not the place where you start.

tasks.label: COMPARE POSITIONS
tasks.prompt: Green is at place 4. Red is at place 7. How many places farther along is red?

math.extension: Wavelength is the space from one wave crest to the next. Imagine how stretched out a drawn wave looks. Along our strip toward red, wavelengths get longer. Which end would have more closely spaced crests?
math.parentNote: Use about 15 minutes for naming, counting, and explaining. Accept pointing, spoken strategies, or drawn hops. UV-A has shorter wavelengths than visible light. This strip samples six color names from a continuous spectrum, omitting indigo as a separate label. Box widths and position numbers are not wavelengths. No nanometers, formulas, or real lamp are needed.

writing.title: Give the glow a path.
writing.intro: Choose one scene. Say what the clue helped Little discover. Draw, label, or write one idea.
writing.draw: Draw a clue from your scene. Add an arrow to show where light goes or a label to name a change.

frames.start: The dark patch was a clue because

frames.hint: What light goes in? What light comes out?

writing.check: Point to the detail your words explain. If you write a sentence, check its first capital and ending mark.
writing.parentNote: About 15 minutes: talk for 3, draw for 4, write for 6, read back for 2. Welcome speech, dictation, invented spelling, or a labeled drawing. Write Leo's words as he says them. One careful idea is enough.

parentGuidance: Let a guess come first. This is a screen and paper exploration; no real lamp or chemical experiment is needed. Ordinary black lights mainly use near-ultraviolet UV-A, not X-rays. Adults manage real UV equipment; never aim it at eyes or skin. UV-A is invisible; visible violet leakage is separate. Fluorescence promptly re-emits absorbed energy as light, usually at a longer wavelength. A phosphor is a luminescent material, not the element phosphorus; the model uses a fluorescent phosphor. Some materials instead keep an afterglow (phosphorescence). Glow depends on both material and lamp wavelength. Ritter and Stokes supplied discoveries on the path to black lights; neither is presented as their sole inventor. The six illustrations are imagined museum scenes. Accept dictation and stop whenever you have had enough.

visualNotes.intent: An unseen-light mystery becomes a visible material clue. Keep Big and Little beside the discovery, with ink, warm paper, dark walnut and rare brass. Color earns its place by showing the mechanism.
visualNotes.grownUpNote: AI-generated scenic illustrations, made with built-in image generation. Historical displays are imagined reconstructions. The interactive lens enlarges a model coating; its dashed UV path is a teaching symbol for invisible light. No image is a measured spectrum, a build plan, or proof that a particular real object fluoresces.
